nodes.body: It is the end-of-season boatyard sale. A thin, steady drizzle turns the air into a wet grey blur. Three tables sit on the gravel, piled with things people no longer want. You find it in a cardboard box of odds and ends: a compass with a chipped enamel face. The metal edge is tarnished a dull green. You almost put it back, but then you tilt it to the light. You see a row of six tiny arrows scratched into the case, each linked by a single, winding line.

choices.label: Open the case and read the card.

nodes.body: Folded into eighths inside the compass case, the card is soft as cloth. It is covered in spidery, water-stained ink. At the top it reads THE LOCK RUN. Under it are six place names. Only half belong to any map you have ever seen of this part of the canal. The last one says WINDING POOL. Someone drew a row of six tiny numbers beneath the names. Four of them are crossed out. You ask the yard manager, a woman called Mrs Okonjo, where the box came from. She says it was from a narrowboat called The Perseverance. Its owner used to navigate the old fly-boat runs.

choices.label: Ask Mrs Okonjo about the boat.
Start at the nearest mark on the casing.
Take the card to the history centre.

nodes.body: Mrs Okonjo has cleared sixteen boats from the yard so far this year. She claims she forgets none of them. The paperwork for this one lives in a waterproof folder shoved under the bench in the dock office. The boat, she tells you, belonged to a man called Harold Stern. He died back in March. She taps her pen on the desk for a moment and then remembers. There is one crate of his things that was so heavy they haven't even priced it yet. It is still in the dry store.

choices.label: Ask to see the unpriced crate.
Look at the photographs properly.
Ask to look round the boat itself.

nodes.body: Held up to the light, the winding line on the casing becomes a stretch of the local canal. The six scratched arrows sit along it in an order that is completely different from the card. The nearest mark is only a fifteen-minute walk away. It is at the old lock-keeper's hut, which is a tea room now. A sign swings over the towpath where a painted number board used to hang. The four bolt holes for the board are still there, rusted and empty.

choices.label: Go to the lock-keeper's hut.
Follow the winding line along the canal.
Look at the iron bridge.

nodes.body: The canal history centre keeps the local records on four shelves and an ancient microfilm reader. It still gobbles up twenty-pence pieces like they are going out of fashion. Behind the desk is someone called Aisha. She has been waiting here the better part of a year for somebody, anybody, to ask her a question. She wants a question with an actual date, not just a vague memory of a boat someone's grandad once owned.

choices.label: Work the local history shelf.
Get the microfilm reader going.
Ask Aisha what she already knows.

nodes.body: The unpriced crate lives under the dock office stairs. It has not been opened for weeks. Inside, there is a cap with a faded blue peak and a badge showing a canal boat. There are two black-and-white photos with eleven names written carefully on the back. There is also a thick paper wallet stuffed with receipts. They are for brass polish, rope, a new bilge pump, and one repaired fog horn.

choices.label: Work out who the names belong to.
Read the receipts for what they say.
Take the cap to somebody who knew it.

nodes.body: Two black-and-white photos show a group of twenty-one people in matching caps. They stand on a set of brick steps somewhere along the canal. On the back, in soft pencil, are eleven names and the words FIRST SATURDAY. You look at those steps for a long time. They are not the steps by the tea room, and they are not anywhere else you can immediately picture. Someone scrubbed their memory right off the towpath.

choices.label: Work out who the names belong to.
Read the receipts for what they say.
Take the cap to somebody who knew it.

nodes.body: The Perseverance sits empty in the wet dock, its key hanging on a hook in the office. There are strict rules about who can be inside and when. Mrs Okonjo knows exactly when you can step aboard and when you absolutely cannot. She will say yes to someone who asks her properly. She will say a flat, hard no to anyone who just wanders in through the stern doors. You take a breath and decide how to play it.

choices.label: Work out who the names belong to.
Read the receipts for what they say.
Take the cap to somebody who knew it.

nodes.body: The old lock-keeper's hut is a tea room now, with a striped awning and a sandwich board. The only thing left of its old job is a strip of iron set into the brickwork right by the lock gate. Beside it, the wall wears a perfect rectangle of cleaner, paler brick. Something the size of a paperback was clearly once fixed there. Then, just as clearly, it was taken off and never put back.

choices.label: Work out what came off the wall.
Look under the paint.
Ask at the lock-side cafe.

nodes.body: The winding line on the casing runs from the old iron bridge all the way down to the winding pool. The six arrows sit along it at distances that match no modern map of the canal at all. You stare at it for ages until you realise why. The map someone drew it from includes a short, lost arm of the canal that was filled in decades ago. You add it back in your head and suddenly the marks make perfect sense.

choices.label: Work out what came off the wall.
Look under the paint.
Ask at the lock-side cafe.

nodes.body: The iron bridge is painted dark green over a hundred older coats of dark green. On the upstream side is an iron plate that says CANAL COMPANY 1903. Right next to it is a smaller, completely bare square of rusted rivets. A second, smaller plate is very obviously not there. The rivets sit there like buttons on an empty coat, holding nothing.

choices.label: Work out what came off the wall.
Look under the paint.
Ask at the lock-side cafe.

nodes.body: Two shelves hold a jumbled run of old canal society newsletters. Their spines are as soft as damp paper. You pick up the volume from December 1961. You find a single paragraph about the Lock Run that lists all six stops in an order you have not seen before. It does not match the card. It does not match the compass casing either. You now have three competing sets of clues in your hands.

choices.label: Look at the plate in the drawer.
Find the canal trust minutes.
Find out when the clearance happens.

nodes.body: You put twenty pence in the microfilm reader. It whirs into life. It holds the local paper back to 1892. Every December edition has a grainy photo. The photo shows people by the snow-dusted canal in heavy coats. They hold brass fog horns and life rings. They hold them like they are precious, fragile things they are scared of dropping.

choices.label: Look at the plate in the drawer.
Find the canal trust minutes.
Find out when the clearance happens.

nodes.body: Aisha has been behind this desk for four years. She keeps a drawer full of things people brought in to get a name for. They gave them in a rush and never came back. Right at the bottom of this drawer is a dull brass plate wrapped in an old freezer bag. The plate is about the size of a paperback. It has four holes in it and no clue what it is for. It has been waiting here for nine months for someone like you.

choices.label: Look at the plate in the drawer.
Find the canal trust minutes.
Find out when the clearance happens.

nodes.body: There are eleven names on the back of a photo. They are written in a careful, strange hand. Three of these names are still on nameplates on boats along this part of the canal. One is painted in bold, curling letters on the front of the lock-side cafe. A name on a photo is just a bit of someone's past. It stays that way until you find a living person to go with it. You know you have to start knocking on boat hatches.

choices.label: Find out who Harold Stern was.
Go and find Bill Hurst.
Search the boat before it is cleared.

nodes.body: A receipt is a boring scrap of paper, but it also cannot lie. A new bilge pump in 1989. A fog horn repaired in 1994. And then, tucked at the back, a locksmith called out to the store room beneath the old lock-keeper's hut in November 1998, just six weeks before the Lock Run was held for the very last time.

choices.label: Put the six stops into the right order.
Leave the crate and come back tomorrow.
Find out who Harold Stern was.

nodes.body: The cap has a faded blue peak and a tiny brass badge. The badge shows a narrowboat crossing a lock. There are maybe four people left on this whole canal who would know that badge in a busy tea room. One lives in the sheltered moorings by the allotments. One is a man called Bill Hurst.

choices.label: Go and find Bill Hurst.
Search the boat before it is cleared.
Put the six stops into the right order.

nodes.body: There is a rectangle of cleaner brick beside the lock gate. It is the exact size of a paperback and has four holes in it. You have seen enough to know that every missing plate was that exact size. Somewhere along the canal is a dusty shed with five brass plates in a box. Or, more likely, there is a skip from 1998 that took the lot.

choices.label: Measure the marks against a real map.
Go up to the chapel steps.
Try the old moorings garden.

nodes.body: A brass plate painted over five times is still a plate underneath. The difference only really shows in a raking light or if you run your thumbnail slowly across the surface. There are two walls on this route where the paint sits proudly on top of a hidden shape instead of lying flat against the brick, and one of those walls is directly behind the cafe's menu board.

choices.label: Go and look at the winding pool.
Walk the whole route and leave it at that.
Measure the marks against a real map.

nodes.body: The wall of the lock-side cafe has a heavy wooden menu board. It is screwed into the brickwork at the exact height a small brass plate would have been fixed. The owner, Deniz, has never looked behind it. The cafe is packed full from eleven until three. Then it is totally empty for one hour before the teatime rush. You work out exactly when that hour is.

choices.label: Go up to the chapel steps.
Try the old moorings garden.
Go and look at the winding pool.

nodes.body: The brass plate reads LOCK THE THIRD. Under it is a single, deeply stamped number. On the back, someone has scratched a name and a date from autumn 1998. Aisha tells you plainly that it came in with a house clearance. It has been in this drawer for nine long months. She says it was waiting for just this talk and no one else.

choices.label: Work out what the six numbers are for.
Go and see Mr Vance at the waterways depot.
Search the paper for the last run.

nodes.body: The canal trust minutes live in a dusty box file. The file smells of old paper and damp. They are the dullest reading you have ever done. On page four of the February set is a single, exciting line. It is buried in a long report about nothing. The line is about clearing the store room under the lock-keeper's hut. This is before the summer fix-up works.

choices.label: Ring the number on the minutes.
Build the file first and act on it later.
Work out what the six numbers are for.

nodes.body: The list says the boat must be cleared this Friday. The work barge is already booked. When a store room that has been ignored for years is finally cleared, it is cleared for good. Anything still under the lock-keeper's hut will go into a dumpster and then the tip. No one in charge will ever know what was lost.

choices.label: Go and see Mr Vance at the waterways depot.
Search the paper for the last run.
Ring the number on the minutes.

nodes.body: Harold Stern ran the fly-boat runs for thirty-one years. He never once missed a Lock Run. He kept every receipt, note, and letter he ever got. Yet he lived on a boat with only one shelf of books. Not a single photo hung on the walls. The other boaters on the moorings knew his name and almost nothing else. That quietness feels like its own piece of proof.

choices.label: Go and look hard at the padlock.
Count what the six numbers must be.
Take everything to Bill Hurst.

nodes.body: Bill Hurst was the last captain of the Lock Run. He lives on a houseboat just past the old boatyard. Everyone you ask about him says the same two things in the same order. They say he is not as sharp as he once was, and that you should go and talk to him anyway. You wonder if he has ever seen the compass, or if he will even know what it means.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to hold the clearance.
Get behind the cafe menu board.
Ask at the sheltered moorings.

nodes.body: There is only one afternoon left before The Perseverance is emptied and towed away. On any old boat, the places worth checking are always the same. There is the top of the wardrobe, the back of the electric cupboard, and that dark, dusty gap behind the bottom drawer in the galley. Every liveaboard for the last hundred years has shoved the one thing they did not want thrown away into that spot.

choices.label: Ask about the cage at the depot.
Get into the chapel.
Ask at the community centre about the gear.

nodes.body: The card lists six places in one order. The scratched arrows on the compass casing list them in a whole other order. One of those orders is the way the boaters walked the route in the cold, with horns sounding across the water. The other is the order someone wrote them in later, at a table, from memory. You just have to work out which is which.

choices.label: Write to the local paper.
Get Tess and her bike into it.
Work backwards from Friday morning.

nodes.body: You lay the compass marks over a real map of the canal, using a ruler and a pencil. Five of the six marks fall within thirty paces of something solid. But the sixth mark lands right in the middle of the new supermarket. This means one of two things. Either the person who scratched the compass made a stupid mistake. Or the supermarket was built on top of something important that everyone has since forgotten.

choices.label: Go and look hard at the padlock.
Count what the six numbers must be.
Take everything to Bill Hurst.

nodes.body: The chapel steps are wide and worn smooth in the middle by a century of feet. They are clearly the exact steps from the photograph. The brick wall beside them has four plugged holes at plate height. The mortar in the holes is a slightly different grey from the rest. It looks like whoever did the job was in a hurry and hoped nobody would ever check.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to hold the clearance.
Get behind the cafe menu board.
Ask at the sheltered moorings.

nodes.body: The sheltered moorings garden is through an old arch off the basin. On its far wall is a small brass rectangle. It is exactly the right size. It sits half hidden behind a huge, overgrown climbing rose that nobody has pruned since it first seemed like a good idea. Everyone who lives here stopped seeing it years ago. Now it is just part of the view.

choices.label: Ask about the cage at the depot.
Get into the chapel.
Ask at the community centre about the gear.

nodes.body: The lock-keeper's hut sits at the head of the winding pool. Its old paint is flaking off in thick curls. A heavy steel door is set into the brick arch right under it. A six-wheel padlock hangs from a rusty hasp on the door, gone green-grey with age. Somebody in a temper attacked the lock with a screwdriver and then gave up. The faint, angry scratch marks are still there.

choices.label: Write to the local paper.
Get Tess and her bike into it.
Work backwards from Friday morning.

nodes.body: Six stops on the run, six brass plates, one number punched onto each, and a six-wheel padlock on a steel door. Four of the numbers on the card are crossed out in the exact same ink as the rest, which means somebody stood in front of that door and tried, got it wrong four times, and then stopped. They didn't solve it. They just gave up and scribbled their failure onto the card as a warning.

choices.label: Go and look hard at the padlock.
Count what the six numbers must be.
Take everything to Bill Hurst.

nodes.body: Mr Vance runs the waterways depot from a dusty yard behind the leisure centre. He has a clipboard, a small van, and a contractor's barge already booked for Friday morning at eight. He has also been told twice this year, very firmly, by people above him, that everything in that store room is worthless junk from before the flood defences went in. You can see he half-believes them.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to hold the clearance.
Get behind the cafe menu board.
Ask at the sheltered moorings.

nodes.body: The last Lock Run was on the first Saturday of December 1998, in driving sleet that froze on the towpath wire. The local paper gave it just four column inches and a slightly blurred photo. It showed eleven people by the winding pool where once there had been twenty-one. The caption underneath just says 'The Lock Run gathers for the final time.' No one said why.

choices.label: Ask about the cage at the depot.
Get into the chapel.
Ask at the community centre about the gear.

nodes.body: The number at the bottom of the trust minutes rings a desk inside the council. The desk has changed teams twice since the document was printed. The person who finally answers the phone is friendly, truly helpful, and has no power at all to say yes. But they can tell you exactly which one person in the council does have that power. It feels like progress.

choices.label: Write to the local paper.
Get Tess and her bike into it.
Work backwards from Friday morning.

nodes.body: The unpriced crate gets shoved into a general lot on Thursday, along with a dozen other boxes from the clear-out. By the time anyone knows what was inside it, the cap, photos, and receipts are gone. They have been scattered to three different second-hand shops across the county. The compass stays, and the card stays. But every other real thing that could have helped you prove any of it is now long gone. The trail is still there, but the proof is not.

The six marks turn out to be six real places along a very damp and windswept part of the canal. The walk between them in the drizzle takes the best part of two hours and answers nothing. You find four bare, dripping walls, a car park, and a single stubborn padlock. It is a brilliant, careful map of a waterway that has moved on. The compass goes back into its case so you can go home and dry off.

ending.title: Six Marks and a Wet Afternoon

nodes.body: By five to five, you have put together a neat folder. It holds the six stops, the dates from the receipts, the trust minutes, and a copy of the brass plate. It is solid, well-researched work, and you are proud of it. Still, the barge comes on Friday morning. The folder gets put on the local history shelf. In about twenty years, somebody else will find it and wonder if it was ever almost solved.

The door under the lock-keeper's hut is heavy steel set in a damp brick arch. The padlock has six wheels and its surface is spotted a sickly green from years of rain and canal spray. You crouch down and try it. The first two wheels turn freely under your thumb. The last four are stiff, gritty, and hard to move. This small fact feels more solid and useful than a whole day of guessing.

choices.label: Walk down to the canal and think.
Sit on the lock-keeper's steps and lay it all out.
Go home and look at the compass under a lamp.

nodes.body: Six stops on the route, six brass plates on six walls, and one number on each. The card has four crossed out in the same angry ink. The library plate says LOCK THE THIRD and gives up one single number. You are left with finding the right walking order and four complete unknowns. It is like having most of a jigsaw but no picture on the box.

choices.label: Go after the plates themselves.
Go after the people who were there.
Go after the paperwork.

nodes.body: Bill Hurst is eighty-four and lives on his houseboat. Sometimes he cannot even hold onto what day it is. And yet, you sit with him for just five minutes. He can still name every single turn on the old fly-boat run. He can hum every note of the horn call they used to start the Lock Run without pausing once to think.

choices.label: Split the route with Tess.
Work backwards from Friday morning.
Sit down with Bill and the photographs.

nodes.body: Halting a booked clearing for a day costs Mr Vance one slightly awkward phone call. It means a bit of grumbling from the man on the barge, and one extra note on his form. The only thing that ever made him make that call is someone turning up with a real, solid reason. A hopeful feeling in their pocket is not enough.

choices.label: Walk down to the canal and think.
Sit on the lock-keeper's steps and lay it all out.
Go home and look at the compass under a lamp.

nodes.body: Four rusty screws, a wooden menu board, and a bit of wall not really looked at since 1994. Deniz agrees to unscrew it at half past two. That is the dead quiet between lunch and the kids coming in for cake after school. He will not do it at half past five when half the town lines up for chips and tea.

choices.label: Go after the plates themselves.
Go after the people who were there.
Go after the paperwork.

nodes.body: Eleven people live here. On a Tuesday afternoon a fresh tin of biscuits sits open on the table. Among them are two who stood on that frozen towpath for the very last Lock Run. One even has the photo of it, the one with sleet blurring their faces, framed on the wall of her tiny hall. Their memories are patchy but completely real.

choices.label: Split the route with Tess.
Work backwards from Friday morning.
Sit down with Bill and the photographs.

nodes.body: The waterways depot keeps any removed fixings in a locked mesh cage behind the salt bin. This system runs on a kind of unofficial memory. No one has ever been asked to explain the filing logic out loud. You find out that the brass plate from the iron bridge came away during the repaint in 2001. It was just shoved in there. It is still there.

choices.label: Walk down to the canal and think.
Sit on the lock-keeper's steps and lay it all out.
Go home and look at the compass under a lamp.

nodes.body: The chapel is locked tight on weekdays and the key lives with the warden. He is out until four and will not be hurried. The steps outside it, though, are clearly the steps from the 1961 photo. You stand on them, feeling the worn dips in the stone. You see this is the first thing you have proved today. It feels solid under your feet.

choices.label: Go after the plates themselves.
Go after the people who were there.
Go after the paperwork.

nodes.body: Half the local boaters think the old safety gear and horns went to the community centre in 1998. The other half are sure a dealer bought the lot for scrap. You check the centre's storage cupboard anyway. Behind a stack of plastic chairs, you find a huge, old fog horn. CANAL LOCK RUN is stencilled in faded white letters down its brass bell. It weighs a ton.

choices.label: Split the route with Tess.
Work backwards from Friday morning.
Sit down with Bill and the photographs.

nodes.body: The local paper prints on a Thursday and comes out on Friday morning. Their letter deadline is Wednesday lunchtime. One small but well-placed paragraph from you would land in three hundred kitchens on the very day the barge comes to empty the store room. It would be read with tea and toast exactly one day too late to help.

choices.label: Walk down to the canal and think.
Sit on the lock-keeper's steps and lay it all out.
Go home and look at the compass under a lamp.

nodes.body: Tess can cover the whole length of the canal in forty minutes flat on her rusty old bike. She has no time at all for standing in polite doorways and making small talk with grown-ups. She is either the single best tool for this mad afternoon, or the exact wrong one. You think about it for a second and decide it doesn't matter. You need the speed.

choices.label: Go after the plates themselves.
Go after the people who were there.
Go after the paperwork.

nodes.body: The barge is booked for eight on Friday morning. That looks scary written in a notebook. But you work it out in hours: you have two whole afternoons, one evening, and all of Thursday. Once you see it as a list of free time rather than a messy pile of worries, it stops feeling hopeless. It feels tight, but you can do it.

choices.label: Split the route with Tess.
Work backwards from Friday morning.
Sit down with Bill and the photographs.

nodes.body: The towpath at four in the afternoon is empty except for a few ducks. The water in the canal is the colour of cold, stewed tea. You walk the whole length of it once, slowly. The compass is in your pocket and the damp air is on your face. By the time you reach the winding pool, the six problems you started with have quietly become just one problem. It has an order to it.

choices.label: Get the menu board off the cafe wall.

nodes.body: The steps of the lock-keeper's hut stay perfectly dry under the overhang. They are wide enough for you to lay out the card, the plate, the photos, and the receipts all at once, side by side. Spread out in the dull, flat light like this, they stop being a collection of odd bits. They start looking like a proper, urgent list. You can see what needs to happen first.

choices.label: Sit down with Bill Hurst.

nodes.body: Under the strong yellow light of the kitchen lamp, the compass casing gives up one more tiny detail that the grey daylight outside never revealed. It is a seventh scratch, and it is not a place at all. It is a small, very carefully carved arrow, pointing deliberately back towards the very first mark on the route. It is a loop. A return. A clue you almost missed.

choices.label: Read the waterways minutes properly.

nodes.body: Five walls, one locked depot cage, and one huge, overgrown rose bush stand between you and six brass rectangles. A plate in your hand is a real number that nobody can argue with. That is worth more in this busy week than being told things by people who are only half-sure. You put your rucksack on and decide to hunt them down.

choices.label: Get the menu board off the cafe wall.
Find the plate in the sheltered moorings garden.
Look in the cage at the waterways depot.

nodes.body: Twenty-one people stood on those brick steps back in 1961. Eleven of them stood in the sleet for the last one in 1998. The ones who are still around are within a mile of your bench. They are mostly indoors. Most of them, you suspect, would be quietly glad to be asked. People like this often are, if you just take the time to knock.

choices.label: Check the chapel steps for fixing holes.
Sit down with Bill Hurst.
Talk to the sheltered moorings residents.

nodes.body: The store room under the lock-keeper's hut supposedly belongs to somebody, on a form, somewhere. The clearance itself is just a single line buried in a set of trust minutes. Both of those things are just bits of paper. Bits of paper can be changed by the right sentence landing in the right ear before the barge arrives on Friday. You just have to find the ear.

choices.label: Talk to Deniz at the cafe.
Ask at the community centre about the gear.
Read the waterways minutes properly.

nodes.body: Two people can cover the upper and lower parts of the canal at the same time. They can get through twice as many clues. But they each learn only half of the story. The whole plan only works if there is a fixed time and a dry bench agreed in advance. That is for putting the two halves of the search back together. You text Tess a time and a place.

choices.label: Search the paper for December 1998.
Find out who owns the store room.
Write to somebody who can stop Friday.

nodes.body: Eight o'clock on Friday morning. A flat barge, two men in overalls, and a skip. Everything you do between now and then either pushes that moment back or it doesn't. Write it down as a strict countdown of hours you have left. It sorts all the possible jobs in your head. The truly useful ones separate from the just interesting ones. You circle the urgent ones in red.

choices.label: Get the menu board off the cafe wall.
Find the plate in the sheltered moorings garden.
Look in the cage at the waterways depot.

nodes.body: Photos work on Bill in a way that direct questions simply do not. Give one of the old black-and-white prints to him and the names come back perfectly, in the order they walked, with the horn calls attached. The trick is to have your wits about you and a pen ready before he starts. He does not pause and he will not repeat himself for a notebook.

choices.label: Check the chapel steps for fixing holes.
Sit down with Bill Hurst.
Talk to the sheltered moorings residents.

nodes.body: Four screws, a heavy wooden menu board, and a bit of wall nobody has properly checked since 1994. Deniz holds the board while you work. Behind it, untouched for decades, is a patch of redder, older brick with the brass plate still fixed firmly to it. It has been painted over with the same cream paint as the rest of the cafe. The number on it is only just readable if you run your thumb across it.

choices.label: Clean the paint off carefully.
Read what the plate actually says.
Ask before anything comes off a wall.

nodes.body: The sheltered moorings wall has a brass plate that no one who lives there sees anymore. It is half hidden by an old climbing rose no one ever cuts back. The residents' group holds very strong, detailed views on the rose's future. Their views go back even further than the Lock Run itself.

choices.label: Take a rubbing instead of the plate.
Get Mr Vance to open the depot cage.
Take the chapel plate off and read it indoors.

nodes.body: The locked mesh cage behind the salt bin at the depot is a complete jumble. It holds forty bent street signs, a broken bench end, and four fancy iron bits from the old bridge. There is a mouldy cardboard box stuffed full of small, tarnished brass objects. Nobody has ever listed them since the system was invented. You could be looking at the missing plate right now.

choices.label: Clean the paint off carefully.
Read what the plate actually says.
Ask before anything comes off a wall.

nodes.body: Four neatly filled holes sit at plate height beside the chapel steps. They are plugged with mortar that has worn to a shade slightly too pale for the old brick around it. You track down the warden who filled them. He is the one who is out until four. When you finally catch him, he admits he remembers doing it. He even remembers the look of the plate he took down.

choices.label: Take a rubbing instead of the plate.
Get Mr Vance to open the depot cage.
Take the chapel plate off and read it indoors.

nodes.body: You put a photo into Bill Hurst's large, worn hands. Twenty-one names come back in perfect order, with the horn calls like a soundtrack. Then you ask him what day it is. The room goes quiet while he hunts for the answer. Both of these things are true at the same time. One fact does not cancel out the other. The man in the photo is still here, just patchy.

choices.label: Chase the eleven names on the photograph.
Go back to Bill with the rubbings.
Ask Bill to show you the compass marking.

nodes.body: It's a Tuesday afternoon with eleven residents and a good tin of shortbread going around. You learn that two people here stood on the towpath in the sleet for the very last Lock Run. And a third person, a woman in a green cardigan, has the news photo of it framed on her shelf. It's right outside her door.

choices.label: Find Harold Stern's family.
Let the common room talk itself out.
Take the first confident answer and run with it.

nodes.body: Deniz got the cafe from his uncle, who took it over from the old coal wharf. Everything that came with the building is stuffed in a carrier bag in the cellar. The bag has unread papers from the eighties and a small, unmarked key. It doesn't seem to fit any lock that anyone knows. He hands you the key and shrugs. 'Maybe it opens the past,' he says, then goes back to the fryer.

choices.label: Chase the eleven names on the photograph.
Go back to Bill with the rubbings.
Ask Bill to show you the compass marking.

nodes.body: The centre's storage cupboard holds a huge, dusty fog horn. CANAL LOCK RUN is stencilled down the side of its brass bell. No one who works there now will say how it got there. They don't know whose it is. And no one knows why it has been silent for twenty-eight years. They just found it one day behind the badminton nets.

choices.label: Find Harold Stern's family.
Let the common room talk itself out.
Take the first confident answer and run with it.

nodes.body: Page four, item nine. A single, dry sentence says to clear the store room beneath the lock-keeper's hut. This was needed for the summer works that are long overdue. At the bottom of the page, there's a scrawled name, a department code, and a chillingly bland note. The group simply 'noted' the action. They noted it and did nothing else.

choices.label: Read what the storage sentence promised.
Get photocopies of everything.
Find the one person who can say yes.

nodes.body: Four column inches, a grainy photo of eleven people in the sleet, and one last hopeful paragraph. It says all the gear would stay in the lock-keeper's hut until the Lock Run could start again. Somebody typed that sentence, printed it, and truly meant it then. It has just taken twenty-eight years for anyone to read it again.

choices.label: Fill in the form the proper way.
Get Aisha to write what the history centre wants.
Send it in and wait for an answer.

nodes.body: The lock-keeper's hut is trust property, and the store room beneath it is trust property, but the old navigational gear stored inside it may not legally be either. This is a messy, crucial distinction that nobody in the history of the canal has ever thought to put in writing. If it belongs to the original crew, then clearing it is taking something that isn't theirs.

choices.label: Read what the storage sentence promised.
Get photocopies of everything.
Find the one person who can say yes.

nodes.body: A letter that arrives on Thursday is a letter that arrives far too late to stop anyone. So this approach has to be an email, followed by a phone call, followed by a real person physically standing in a doorway. And only the third of those three things, as you have already discovered this week, has ever, in the history of the canal, actually moved a booked contractor.

choices.label: Fill in the form the proper way.
Get Aisha to write what the history centre wants.
Send it in and wait for an answer.

nodes.body: You need patience, a wooden coffee stirrer, and no sharp metal tools at all. Paint comes off old brass this way. Twenty wrong seconds with a scraper will ruin a brass plate that sat quietly for sixty years. It will leave a deep, angry cut right through the number. Your hands need to be very still for this.

choices.label: Line up the five you have.
Work out where the sixth one went.
Ask about the lockers nobody ever clears.

nodes.body: It says LOCK THE FIFTH. Under it is a single figure that is either a 3 or an 8. It depends only on the angle of the grey towpath light. This is the sort of maddening, unclear problem that a six-wheel combo lock does not forgive. There is no room for error. You stare at it and your heart sinks slightly.

choices.label: Show the numbers to Bill Hurst.
Put back everything that came off a wall.
Line up the five you have.

nodes.body: A brass plate on a brick wall belongs to the wall. The wall belongs to someone who pays insurance. The gap between pausing to ask them first, or just going ahead, is huge. It is the gap between being helped all week by people who trust you, and getting angry phone calls by Thursday. It is a tightrope you now have to walk.

choices.label: Work out where the sixth one went.
Ask about the lockers nobody ever clears.
Show the numbers to Bill Hurst.

nodes.body: Soft tracing paper and the side of a wax crayon lift the number off a plate cleanly. They do not move the plate a single bit. A rubbing can be taken to Bill Hurst's houseboat. You can photo it in good light and argue over it at the table. No one needs to be legally in charge of unbolting a piece of canal history. It is the safest tool you have.

choices.label: Put back everything that came off a wall.
Line up the five you have.
Work out where the sixth one went.

nodes.body: The cage at the depot has its own strong padlock. Mr Vance keeps the key on a huge ring with about forty others. He will open it for you. But first, before he even reaches for his belt, he wants a clear reason. He wants a proper name to put against it. And he wants about four minutes of you being very straight with him. No bluffing will work in this yard.

choices.label: Ask about the lockers nobody ever clears.
Show the numbers to Bill Hurst.
Put back everything that came off a wall.

nodes.body: Eleven names are written on the back of the photo. Four of those people have died. Three moved away years ago. Two live in the sheltered moorings. One stands behind the counter at the lock-side cafe. And one is, of course, Bill Hurst. Finding all that out takes a whole afternoon. You walk the towpath and have eight polite talks with strangers.

choices.label: Check a memory against a document.
Bring two of them down to the winding pool.
Ask who had the key in 1998.

nodes.body: You spread the brass rubbings across the little table on his houseboat. They do what your string of questions could not. Bill reads the numbers aloud without pause. Then he reads the names of the locks. Then, with a small, sad snort of laughter, he tells you which lock the crew always got wrong. They miscounted it every single year, halfway through the run.

choices.label: Slow down and do it their way.
Write down what people say while they say it.
Check a memory against a document.

nodes.body: He takes the compass from you and just looks at the casing for a long, quiet moment. Then, without any warning, he traces the winding scratch with his thumb, following it. He describes an old, low horn signal, a short pattern of notes, that the crew used to sound before setting off. He says the scratch isn't a mark, it's a notation, and it has been there since 1961.

choices.label: Bring two of them down to the winding pool.
Ask who had the key in 1998.
Slow down and do it their way.

nodes.body: Harold Stern has a niece living in Wales. She has never even visited the canal. But she is very keen to talk about an uncle nobody has asked her about for eleven years. Her voice wobbles a little as she tells you she has two whole boxes of his old things. They sit untouched in her loft.

choices.label: Write down what people say while they say it.
Check a memory against a document.
Bring two of them down to the winding pool.

nodes.body: Asking a sharp, direct question in this common room gets you one unsure answer. And it is not a very good one. But letting the room talk loosely for twenty minutes while the biscuits go round gets you nine answers. Four are mixed-up myths. But two are tiny, sparkling facts. Nobody would ever have thought to ask for them in a direct way.

choices.label: Ask who had the key in 1998.
Slow down and do it their way.
Write down what people say while they say it.

nodes.body: 'Stored until the Lock Run can be restarted.' A trust does not use a sentence like that by accident. You find it printed in the old paper. It is typed in the minutes from 1999. It is even written on a yellowed card taped inside the store room door. You can see it in a photo from 2004. Someone truly meant for it all to come back out one day.

choices.label: Work the clearance date itself.
Find an adult who will carry it inside.
Answer the question they will ask.

nodes.body: It costs twenty pence a sheet at the history centre. Aisha will stamp the date on the back of everything for you. You spread out the receipts, the minutes, the photo, and the card. A real paper copy with an official date stamp does serious, solid work in a meeting. A phone screen held up across a desk never works as well. You slide the stack into a folder.

choices.label: Give the paper something to print.
Ask for ten minutes rather than a decision.
Work the clearance date itself.

nodes.body: Four people inside the trust are in charge of the clearance decision. Through very careful phone calls, you learn that three of them can only say no. Finding the strange fourth person, the one who might say yes, takes two more calls. It also takes the nerve to ask a plain, simple question: 'Who is really allowed to decide this?'

choices.label: Find an adult who will carry it inside.
Answer the question they will ask.
Give the paper something to print.

nodes.body: Buried on the trust website is a special form. You use it to ask the council to keep something they planned to throw away. It is two sides long. It wants a clear reason in less than a hundred words. Nobody has ever quietly explained to you that those hundred words are the whole argument. You sit down with a pen and choose them very carefully.

choices.label: Ask for ten minutes rather than a decision.
Work the clearance date itself.
Find an adult who will carry it inside.

nodes.body: The history centre makes a big change. It formally declares it would take and list the Lock Run archive. The talk stops being 'what do we do with this damp old stuff.' It becomes 'where is the right place for this historic collection.' Aisha nods, pulls out a sheet of headed paper, and writes the offer in one crisp, perfect paragraph.

choices.label: Answer the question they will ask.
Give the paper something to print.
Ask for ten minutes rather than a decision.

nodes.body: The plate comes away from the chapel wall with the second screw. A small, weak corner of the brass snaps off in your hand. Now you have a cracked plate and a raw hole in an old brick wall. You must talk to the warden right away, and it goes as badly as it sounds. The number is just about clear. But no one in the room is happy about how you found it.

ending.title: Two Screws and a Cracked Plate

nodes.body: Five honest people each give you a confident but totally different answer about where the third lock was. You spend the whole afternoon trying to pick the right one. By the time someone thinks to check a map or a trust paper to settle it, the history centre is shut. Thursday morning is almost here and you still have no clear answer.

You send the form on Wednesday. An auto-reply says thank you that same afternoon. A real person reads it the next Tuesday. That is four days after a flat barge, two men, and a big skip showed up. They made the whole debate a sad waste of time. The thank-you letter is very polite. It comes in a small envelope with a window.

You have five plates and five hard-won numbers. Their order depends on whether the old Lock Run went clockwise around the basin or the other way, like the card lists them. You suddenly see that these two possible orders clash at three different spots out of six. You have most of the code, but the sequence is still a guess.

choices.label: Settle the order once and for all.
Take the six numbers to the padlock.
Photograph everything before Friday.

nodes.body: The plate from the old lock-keeper's hut came off when they put up the tea room awning. It never made it to the depot's cage. The builder who did the work retired to the east coast years ago. He only picks up his old phone about half the time you call. The last number might just be sitting in his memory, out of reach.

choices.label: Get the clearance held for a week.
Tell the sheltered moorings what you found.
Go to the padlock with five numbers and a guess.

nodes.body: Along this canal, there are maybe nine old storage lockers and dusty boat sheds. They hold everything that was too good to throw out in 1998. The owners know just what is stacked inside. They are in no rush to be hurried by a kid with a compass. You must decide how to talk to them without making them shut their doors on you.

choices.label: Settle the order once and for all.
Take the six numbers to the padlock.
Photograph everything before Friday.

nodes.body: Bill cannot tell you what he had for lunch. But he looks at your set of rubbings and tells you, without blinking, that the third lock used to stand right outside the old coal wharf. Its plate carried the year the canal first opened. You can tell it is not a guess. It is a real memory, and somehow it comes with a horn call and a tune.

choices.label: Get the clearance held for a week.
Tell the sheltered moorings what you found.
Go to the padlock with five numbers and a guess.

nodes.body: Every plate you carefully unscrewed goes right back onto its wall with the right, matching screws. You do this before anything else happens. Doing it properly and with respect costs a full hour. You only had four hours left in the afternoon to start with. But deep down, you know it would be wrong to rush this part.

choices.label: Settle the order once and for all.
Take the six numbers to the padlock.
Photograph everything before Friday.

nodes.body: One person's memory and a printed church paper tell two different stories about the second lock on the run. The paper was printed the very week it happened. The memory has had sixty long years to quietly tidy itself into a neater tale. That does not always mean the printed one is right. But it does mean you have to check it against other sources.

choices.label: Get the order agreed by people who were there.
Ask Bill for the last number.
Take somebody with you to the padlock.

nodes.body: Two people stood on that frozen towpath in 1998. One has a walking stick, and one uses a wheeled frame. You bring them up to the steel door on a bright, cold afternoon for half an hour. They pay no mind to the lock at all. They just start a friendly argument about the year the hasp was fitted and if the padlock was always that colour.

choices.label: Get the community centre to say what it has.
Put Bill in front of Mr Vance.
Let the afternoon be about the people.

nodes.body: Somebody stood in front of this steel door in December 1998. They locked it and put the combo away for safekeeping. A receipt proves a locksmith was paid to come out six weeks before to fit the new padlock. It means a real, live person set those six numbers on a cold, specific day for a specific reason. You just have to find out what that reason was.

choices.label: Get the order agreed by people who were there.
Ask Bill for the last number.
Take somebody with you to the padlock.

nodes.body: This talk with Bill and the others works only at a gentle speed. It is slower than any busy afternoon with a Friday deadline. Moving at their pace costs you a whole hour you don't really have. But it buys you a steady, returning kind of help. It keeps quietly popping up at your elbow days later.

choices.label: Get the community centre to say what it has.
Put Bill in front of Mr Vance.
Let the afternoon be about the people.

nodes.body: Putting a notebook out in the open on the table changes how a room full of people talks. It changes how carefully they choose their words. By your third visit that week, they have begun to politely correct each other's memories for the record. They do it for the notebook, not for you. The history is starting to record itself through them.

choices.label: Get the order agreed by people who were there.
Ask Bill for the last number.
Take somebody with you to the padlock.

nodes.body: A planned clearance can be moved, cancelled, or cut down to just the part of the store room that is truly ruined by water. These three results are three very different asks. They have three very different chances of getting a yes from the trust. You pick how to ask with great care.

choices.label: Put the whole case on one sheet of paper.
Take the ten minutes with Mr Vance.
Ask permission to try the padlock.

nodes.body: Someone already inside the trust building is worth six formal letters from you. Someone who is already trusted on other things. Someone already a bit annoyed about the rushed summer works. Two people in the local canal world fit that. You find out, with a jolt, that one of them is a governor at the community centre.

choices.label: Bring the community centre in as a home for it.
Spend Thursday getting everyone in one room.
Ask for the week and take the answer as final.

nodes.body: The first thing any official asks about an old, damp store room is 'who pays if someone gets hurt in there?' If you have a calm, ready answer, you get a long, helpful chat. If you do not, the door stays firmly and forever shut in your face. You look up the trust's public liability policy.

choices.label: Put the whole case on one sheet of paper.
Take the ten minutes with Mr Vance.
Ask permission to try the padlock.

nodes.body: A photo of a tarnished brass plate, a historic name, an urgent date, and a barge booked for Friday morning. This is the exact kind of story a local paper will take on a slow Wednesday lunchtime. The two people on the trust who most need to read it will read it Friday morning over toast. They needed to read it Thursday. The timing is cruel but the coverage is good.

choices.label: Bring the community centre in as a home for it.
Spend Thursday getting everyone in one room.
Ask for the week and take the answer as final.

nodes.body: No one in charge with a clipboard just says yes to a stranger from the towpath. But quite a lot of them will give you ten minutes on a Thursday morning if you ask clearly. A ten-minute meeting with the real brass plates set on the desk is a whole new thing. It is a much more convincing talk than just waving your hands around for ten minutes.

choices.label: Put the whole case on one sheet of paper.
Take the ten minutes with Mr Vance.
Ask permission to try the padlock.

nodes.body: The old paper, the compass case, and the folded card give you three different orders for the run. Only one of these was actually walked in the sleet by twenty-one people. The tie-breaker is a real canal problem. You see it all at once. Which way around the winding pool could a group really carry a heavy, clumsy fog horn without dropping it in the water?

choices.label: Go down to the door on Thursday evening.
Fix the order before touching the lock.
Fetch Bill Hurst down to the basin.

nodes.body: Six wheels on a wet padlock. Your fingers numb with cold. And only one order to try. Every wrong guess costs you nothing. Nothing but the small, sick, sinking feeling in your stomach. You watch that last, stiff wheel click into the wrong place and the shackle stays stubbornly shut.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to come and watch.
Bring the two residents and the notebook.
Bring a light and something to write on.

nodes.body: A clear photo of a brass plate still fixed to a wall proves, with no argument, just where it was first put up. That barge leaves on Friday morning. After that, you see, a careful photo might be the only proof anyone ever has. The only proof that anything important was ever kept under that damp old hut. You get the camera ready.

choices.label: Line the community centre up to take the gear.
Get the paper to hold the front of page five.
Get the clearance stopped in writing.

nodes.body: You can delay the clearance for just one week. It is just one call to a grumpy builder and one extra line on a form. But it is also a grown-up with power who thinks about it. He will look a bit foolish in front of his boss. All because of a kid who just showed up with five brass plates in a canvas bag. You wonder if he really will do it.

choices.label: Write the list of what should be in there.
Get the plates back on their walls first.
Be there at eight when the barge comes.

nodes.body: The plate half-hidden in their garden turns out to be Lock the Fourth. People have walked past it for decades. All eleven of them would very much like to be told this small, brilliant, local fact before anyone else is. They want to hear it now, in person. That way they hear it first and can tell their own guests about it later.

choices.label: Go down to the door on Thursday evening.
Fix the order before touching the lock.
Fetch Bill Hurst down to the basin.

nodes.body: Four people who really walked the run sit around a table. They have a clean sheet of paper in front of them. After twenty minutes of patient, messy talk, you have an order that three of them will gladly and firmly defend to anyone. The fourth is grumbling it was different in '83. The others just ignore him. This is as close to fixed fact as this canal ever gets.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to come and watch.
Bring the two residents and the notebook.
Bring a light and something to write on.

nodes.body: The sixth and last stop on the run was never a wall at all. It was the lock-keeper's own hut. That was the goal. Its number was never fixed to any brick. If the last digit is still in this world, it is in two places. It is in the head of the man who set the padlock. Or the head of the friend who stood shivering beside him and watched him do it.

choices.label: Line the community centre up to take the gear.
Get the paper to hold the front of page five.
Get the clearance stopped in writing.

nodes.body: Opening a door on trust land with nobody there to see is risky. Opening it with two well-known moorings people and notes in your hand is a much safer story. And the gap between those two stories matters most if the padlock clicks open. You need someone you can trust to watch what happens next.

choices.label: Write the list of what should be in there.
Get the plates back on their walls first.
Be there at eight when the barge comes.

nodes.body: The cupboard at the community centre holds the fog horn, two old hand lamps, and a heavy wooden case. The case has a faded name inside the lid. If you ask a polite question that sounds like you are just curious, not cross, the manager will own up to all of it. He will even let you take a photo.

choices.label: Go down to the door on Thursday evening.
Fix the order before touching the lock.
Fetch Bill Hurst down to the basin.

nodes.body: Mr Vance has been told again and again that the store room just holds wet junk from before the flood works. Then you stand an eighty-four-year-old man in front of him. This man can name every single thing behind that locked door, item by item, in the exact order it was stacked. That is not the kind of thing a clipboard can survive. Mr Vance puts it down on the desk.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to come and watch.
Bring the two residents and the notebook.
Bring a light and something to write on.

nodes.body: Six stops, five brass plates, one grainy photo, and one dry sentence from the trust minutes. Plus one big Friday date that is coming fast. If the whole urgent case does not fit on one side of a single sheet of A4 paper, you know it will fail. A busy official, standing in a drafty hall with coffee in hand, will not get through it. You make the wording tight.

choices.label: Line the community centre up to take the gear.
Get the paper to hold the front of page five.
Get the clearance stopped in writing.

nodes.body: Mr Vance listens to your ten-minute pitch with the board held loosely at his side. Nobody has ever seen him do that before. He asks just two questions when you finish. Both are calm, real things about who will store the gear later and keep it safe. He does not ask if a single word of your story is true.

choices.label: Write the list of what should be in there.
Get the plates back on their walls first.
Be there at eight when the barge comes.

nodes.body: Trying a lock with someone saying you can takes one quick line beforehand. Trying it without takes a line too, but a very different one, said in a whisper. And you can only use it once. You can never say the second one later to any grown-up who might help. You know which one you need to say today.

choices.label: Go down to the door on Thursday evening.
Fix the order before touching the lock.
Fetch Bill Hurst down to the basin.

nodes.body: Old gear in a cupboard is a storage problem. Old gear in a town brass band is a great use of local history. If a head teacher can see a nice photo in the local paper, they will find space for a heavy fog horn by Friday lunch. They will also claim they had that idea all along.

choices.label: Get Mr Vance to come and watch.
Bring the two residents and the notebook.
Bring a light and something to write on.

nodes.body: Getting the moorings folk, the centre, the history staff, Mr Vance, and one man of eighty-four into one room for half an hour is very tricky to set up. It is much harder than any part of the hunt so far. But if you manage it, that half-hour will fix more than all the rest of the mad week put together.

choices.label: Line the community centre up to take the gear.
Get the paper to hold the front of page five.
Get the clearance stopped in writing.

nodes.body: Five plates. Five hard-won numbers. One big hole in the set. And a padlock that wants all six. You snap a photo of the five you have. You write them neatly on a poster and pin it up at the history centre. The barge comes on Friday. The store room is emptied. The sixth number slowly stops mattering to everyone. Everyone but the one person still looking for it on the quiet. That person is you.

The common room fills up on Thursday night with people who have not been in a room together since that cold December in 1998. There is tea. A battered photo album goes round. Bill Hurst traces the scratch on your compass and tells the whole story. The barge still comes on Friday. But no one sitting in that room can truly say the week was thrown away. It was the best week the canal had seen in years.

ending.title: The Crew That Was Still There

nodes.body: The trust says no to the week's delay on Wednesday afternoon. Their reasons are careful and for the law. You have to admit they are about three parts right. The refusal note is very polite and dead set. The store room is cleared on Friday into a waiting barge. But the two boxes of damp papers inside are, at the last moment, sent to the history centre. Someone, at least, asked that one question in time.

ending.title: A Week That Was Not Given

nodes.body: The basin at seven in the evening is blue-grey and empty. The steel door is colder than the wet brick arch around it. The padlock just hangs there, with six wheels and sixty years of tarnish waiting. The barge is booked for eight o'clock in the morning. The whole long week has shrunk down to this one chilly moment in front of the rust.

choices.label: Set the six numbers and pull.
Try the other order.
Look at the door rather than the lock.

nodes.body: There are two possible walking orders and only one padlock. You know that standing right in front of the lock in the cold is the worst place to make the final choice between them. Five calm minutes here with your notebook and a clear head are worth twenty blind, hopeful tries and a numb thumb.

choices.label: Ask Mr Vance to open it himself.
Let Bill set the wheels.
Write down every attempt.

nodes.body: It takes twenty careful minutes to get Bill from his boat to the hut. He needs his heavy coat and a steady arm on each side. He has not stood in this basin after dark since 1998. He stops in the gate for a long moment to look at the hut's shape. Then he nods and walks slowly across the wet grass to the door.

choices.label: Get a light through the gap under the door.
Find out how wet the store room is.
Meet the barge at eight with the folder.

nodes.body: Mr Vance finishes at half four and lives just eight minutes from the basin. Coming back out on a damp Thursday evening, after his tea, to watch a keen kid try an old lock is either the easiest yes of his whole week or the silliest ask he has ever fielded. He stands with his coat collar up and a tiny, unreadable smile.

choices.label: Get the photographer in front of the door.
Phone the community centre before anything else.
Put the trail back the way it was.

nodes.body: Two people stood right here in 1998. One held a walking stick. The other leaned on a wheeled frame. You have a notebook open and ready in your pocket. No matter what happens at this cold, steel door, it will now be seen. People who can stand up and say, clearly, what took place. The truth will have witnesses.

choices.label: Set the last wheel where Bill says.
Write it all down before you try anything.
Get a torch through the gap and look.

nodes.body: A good torch, a sharp pencil, and a bit of paper. The six numbers are on it in your best writing. You have seen cold, clumsy hands and a dim phone screen lose more codes than wrong numbers ever have. You take a breath and set your gear on the low brick wall next to you. Control is all that matters now.

choices.label: Leave it until the morning and see.
Set the six numbers and pull.
Try the other order.

nodes.body: The head of the community centre will say yes to a fog horn and a nice photo. They will say no to a van full of damp, unknown gear that might be unsafe. The ask has to be clear and fair. To be clear, you first must know for sure what is behind this locked door. You need to see inside.

choices.label: Look at the door rather than the lock.
Ask Mr Vance to open it himself.
Let Bill set the wheels.

nodes.body: The paper goes to press at noon on Thursday. A tired staff photographer sighs on the phone. She will come out at eight in the morning if the story has a skip and some real history. That deadline is the one thing in this whole town that will not move. Nothing you can do will delay it even an hour.

choices.label: Write down every attempt.
Get a light through the gap under the door.
Find out how wet the store room is.

nodes.body: A quick, calm phone call moves a booked worker. A single, formal email stops one in their tracks. By Thursday night, only one kind of 'stopped' will last through the harsh truth of a Friday morning. It is a short, typed note that a person in charge has sent and received. You find yourself checking your inbox every few minutes.

choices.label: Meet the barge at eight with the folder.
Get the photographer in front of the door.
Phone the community centre before anything else.

nodes.body: Eleven names, one fog horn, four hand lamps. One heavy wooden gear case, fixed in 1994, and a box of spare brass bits. A full, fair list written in ink before the door opens is worth ten times a scared, shaky list made later from memory. You start the list on a clean sheet of paper, ready to go.

choices.label: Put the trail back the way it was.
Set the last wheel where Bill says.
Write it all down before you try anything.

nodes.body: Five brass plates, five brick walls, a driver borrowed from Mr. Vance's van, and an hour of the damp Thursday evening. Doing this careful job of putting them all back before you touch the lock is the whole point. It is the gap between a town trail people will thank you for, and a clumsy raid that people will just frown at and recall badly.

choices.label: Get a torch through the gap and look.
Leave it until the morning and see.
Set the six numbers and pull.

nodes.body: The barge, two men in overalls, a skip, and a man with a clipboard arrive at eight on a drizzly Friday morning. And one person stands on the towpath in their way with a file of proof. That person is you. You are either a block to a lawful job, or the one clear reason the whole morning goes a new way. It hangs on your first sentence.

choices.label: Try the other order.
Look at the door rather than the lock.
Ask Mr Vance to open it himself.

nodes.body: Six wheels, your fingers numb and blue with the cold, the last one so stiff that it needs your thumbnail to force it around. You set the final digit, take a breath that mists in the air, and pull. The shackle either lifts clear with a small, clean click, or it stays frozen. The sound it makes, if it does lift, is the sound of a tiny brass mechanism giving up an argument it has been having with the weather since 1998.

choices.label: Go in and look properly.
List everything before moving anything.
Get it out of the damp today.

nodes.body: The second possible order takes just forty seconds to set, but the entire weight of the frantic week rests on those forty seconds. There is nobody standing here on this cold towpath who does not feel that weight pressing down on their shoulders. You set the first wheel, then the second, and keep your breathing steady.

choices.label: Offer the lot to the community centre.
Offer the paper to the history centre.
Take the photograph back to the moorings.

nodes.body: The rusty hasp that holds the lock is screwed into a wooden door frame. That frame has sat outside for sixty winters of rain, frost, and canal spray. You suddenly see the difference between a door that is firmly locked and one that is just shut. That difference could be just four rusted wood screws. The question is if anyone is allowed to touch them.

choices.label: Let Bill go in first.
Find out what can be saved.
Settle who it all belongs to.

nodes.body: Mr Vance has heavy bolt croppers in the back of his van. He has the formal right to use them on trust property. The thing that finally gets him to fetch them, you notice, is not your passionate talk about the gear. It is when you quietly read him the exact sentence from the 1999 minutes. It is the part where the committee promised to store it all 'until the Run can be restarted'.

choices.label: Make sure the right people are told first.
Put the plates back and say so publicly.
Get somebody to sound the horn.

nodes.body: Bill's hands are not as steady as in the photo, and his memory is not either. But he takes the lock from you without a word. He sets four of the six wheels in quick, sure flicks. He never once looks at the paper in your hand. Then he stops fully, his thumb frozen on the fifth wheel. The cold air around him goes very still.

choices.label: Keep trying until the wheels give.
Clean the fog horn and hand it to Bill.
Sign the gear over to the community centre.

nodes.body: A six-wheel padlock has a million possible codes. But only about nine that any busy, sensible person would ever set. A running list of what you have tried is the only thing that stops you. It keeps your ninth angry try from just being a cold-fingered repeat of your third one. You pull the notebook out of your pocket and open it to a fresh page.

choices.label: Make the list and let the barge take the rest.
Work out what the numbers actually mean.
Leave it locked and hope somebody listens.

nodes.body: The gap under the steel door is just two fingers deep. You lie flat on the cold towpath and shine the torch through it. The beam catches a rough concrete floor and the dark corner of a wooden case. It also catches something curved and metal. It might have been a fog horn for the last twenty-eight years. Or it might be an old puddle reflecting your light.

choices.label: Go in and look properly.
List everything before moving anything.
Get it out of the damp today.

nodes.body: The brickwork above the door has been wet since the time the first summer fix plans were made and then dropped. The air that seeps out from under the door smells of wet wool and old brass. Whatever is in there has had twenty-eight freezing winters of it and no fresh air at all.

choices.label: Offer the lot to the community centre.
Offer the paper to the history centre.
Take the photograph back to the moorings.

nodes.body: Two men, a flat barge with a skip, and a man with a clipboard who wants the job done. And there you are. You have a folder full of photos, a copy of the trust notes, and five brass plates wrapped in a tea towel. You have about ninety seconds to say the one useful thing that will stop a skip from eating twenty-eight years of local memory.

choices.label: Let Bill go in first.
Find out what can be saved.
Settle who it all belongs to.

nodes.body: A picture man, a fog horn with a burst bell, and an old man of eighty-four in a faded blue cap. You know that is a front page on this canal. A front page on Friday morning is a whole week later than the barge. But it is a year earlier than the slow creep of forgetting that would swallow the story forever.

choices.label: Make sure the right people are told first.
Put the plates back and say so publicly.
Get somebody to sound the horn.

nodes.body: The head of the local centre answers her phone at ten to eight. Friday mornings are just wild like that. She says yes at once to a clear, short list of gear you read out. Then she asks the one real question you were dreading. 'So, who is going to carry it all across the basin?' It is a question that only has a good answer if you thought about it yesterday.

choices.label: Keep trying until the wheels give.
Clean the fog horn and hand it to Bill.
Sign the gear over to the community centre.

nodes.body: Five brass plates go back onto five waiting walls. The card is folded safely back into the compass case. The compass slides into your pocket. Whatever happens at eight o'clock on Friday morning, the basin ends this week with the old Lock Run route fixed on its brickwork. A person could follow it with a map. A person could finally walk it again.

choices.label: Make the list and let the barge take the rest.
Work out what the numbers actually mean.
Leave it locked and hope somebody listens.

nodes.body: The sixth number was never on any wall. It was not a stop number. It was the year the canal first opened, played backwards like an old lock-keeper's joke. Bill says it aloud the way he says a remembered tune. The shackle lifts on your very first pull. The door creaks open onto twenty-eight years of dark. It lets out the quiet, sad smell of damp wool and old brass.

By nine on Thursday night, you have a single sheet of paper. It holds six stops, six numbers, both walking paths, and every single source written neatly next to each. A copy goes through the door of the history centre with a short note. No matter what happens at eight in the morning, the solved trail is now a fact on paper. It cannot be thrown into a skip.

Behind the door, in the torchlight, there is a fog horn with a burst bell. There are four heavy wooden cases and a stack of old signal books. One damp edge of the books has turned to grey pulp. A card taped to the inside of the door reads, 'The crew will be back.' It is less than the basin recalled and far more than the trust was ever told was down here.

The barge comes early. The men are quick and they work well. The store room is totally empty by twenty past eight. The skip leaves the basin at nine o'clock. A heavy fog horn is inside it. Nobody thought to take a photo first. The open padlock, still locked, hangs on the hasp. The drizzle starts again.

The floor is concrete. The room smells of old brass polish and damp that has outlasted all who used the gear. Four wooden cases are stacked along the back wall. A huge fog horn rests on its side. The weak grey light from the open door only reaches halfway across the room. The rest is just shadow and the hint of shapes.

choices.label: Ask what it would take to start it again.
Get the twenty-one names onto something permanent.
Find out whose case it is.

nodes.body: A list made in a cold doorway with a torch in your teeth is a thousand times more reliable than a list made afterwards from a shaky memory. And this list you are writing, now, in this moment, is going to be the only proper document that will ever exist about a room that has not been opened, or even glanced at, since that sleeting Saturday in December 1998.

choices.label: Hand everything over properly, with paper.
Get the paper to the history centre as an archive.
Make the Lock Run walkable again.

nodes.body: This room has had twenty-eight damp winters to soak into its bones. Another two weeks of waiting while adults argue in a meeting room would ruin more stuff than moving it out today into the dry. Moving it needs four steady hands, a clear dry floor to lay things on, and someone with a clipboard saying a firm 'yes' before the rain gets heavier.

choices.label: Decide what happens to the compass.
Say thank you to everybody who helped.
Set a date for the first Saturday in December.

nodes.body: A community centre with a fog horn and four hand lamps in its storeroom is a centre with a brass band in two years' time. But the same centre with a van full of damp, mouldy cases is just a caretaker with a long, angry grievance. Which version it ends up being is decided this afternoon, in the way you present it. It is all about the first impression.

choices.label: Put the poster up and see who comes.
Get the names onto the lock-keeper's hut.
Track down the name inside the case.

nodes.body: The old signal books, the minute book, and the fading photos are an archive, not a prop. Aisha at the history centre has a proper acid-free box, shelf space, and her heavy date stamp. All are waiting for this delivery. She takes the first box from your arms as if you are handing her treasure.

choices.label: Do the handover on paper, in front of everybody.
Give Aisha the archive she asked for.
Leave the menu board off and let people see.

nodes.body: There is a large group photo in the store room from 1961 with twenty-one names on the back. Two of the people in the picture live just four hundred paces away in the sheltered moorings. They have not seen this photo, or even a copy of it, for sixty years. You roll it with care and tuck it inside your coat to stay dry.

choices.label: Take it to the paper and let the week end.
Ask what it would take to start it again.
Get the twenty-one names onto something permanent.

nodes.body: He stands in the damp doorway for a long while, just looking. Then he starts naming what is inside before the torch beam even reaches it. He lists it in order from the left wall to the right. The list includes a folded music stand exactly where he said it was, behind the door, under a dusty cloth.

choices.label: Find out whose case it is.
Hand everything over properly, with paper.
Get the paper to the history centre as an archive.

nodes.body: A burst horn bell can be fixed with solder. A dull wooden case is just an afternoon's work with a cloth and some wax. But a book of signal patterns gone to grey pulp is sadly lost forever. Knowing which is which needs one calm person who understands old brass gear and about an hour of quiet looking.

choices.label: Make the Lock Run walkable again.
Decide what happens to the compass.
Say thank you to everybody who helped.

nodes.body: The Lock Run was a club, the club had a committee, and it simply stopped meeting one year. What that means for a heavy fog horn locked in a trust store room is a messy, tricky question. Nobody in the whole history of the canal has ever had to answer it out loud. You are the first person to properly ask.

choices.label: Set a date for the first Saturday in December.
Put the poster up and see who comes.
Get the names onto the lock-keeper's hut.

nodes.body: The list of people who should hear about a find like this before the local paper is very short. Everyone on it is over seventy. Getting the order of those visits right costs you one damp evening of walking door-to-door. But it buys you about thirty years of quiet goodwill from the people who recall the real thing.

choices.label: Track down the name inside the case.
Do the handover on paper, in front of everybody.
Give Aisha the archive she asked for.

nodes.body: Six brass plates go back on six brick walls. A short, clear note in the local paper tells everyone what the route really was. It turns a lost, private trail on an old compass into something the whole basin can walk. On a dry Saturday you can follow it with a photocopied map and a flask of tea.

choices.label: Leave the menu board off and let people see.
Take it to the paper and let the week end.
Ask what it would take to start it again.

nodes.body: There is a fog horn in there that will make a low, sad noise with an hour of careful cleaning. There is a man standing right here who can still sound it, despite everything. And there is a winding pool with a broad, grassy bank right in the middle, doing nothing at all. You look at the horn, then at Bill, then back at the horn.

choices.label: Get the twenty-one names onto something permanent.
Find out whose case it is.
Hand everything over properly, with paper.

nodes.body: The third order is the one printed in the old canal club news from 1961. It opens the padlock at twenty past seven on Thursday evening. Two local people watch, a notebook held open in the cold. An eighty-four-year-old man stands back on the grass behind you. Nobody says a word for a long, frozen moment. The only sound is the lock clicking open.

An hour with a clean rag and a bottle of brass polish. Bill Hurst sounds the fog horn on the lock-keeper's steps on a Thursday evening in front of six people. It is a low, long, sad note that rolls across the basin. Three windows in the sheltered moorings swing open. They stay open until he finally lowers the horn and the echo dies.

The head of the community centre signs for one fog horn, four hand lamps, a heavy wooden case, and two metal music stands. This happens on the very Friday morning when the barge was booked. The barge only takes the true, water-damaged rubbish. By next summer, a small, eager, and honestly quite terrible community brass band is practising.

The store room is emptied on time. But because you made the list first, a fog horn, four cases, a minute book, and a box of photos come out safely before the skip does. Everything else goes. It is not the magic week anyone secretly hoped for. And it is not the week that would have happened if you had started on Monday. But it is not a total loss, either.

The six numbers are a date. It is written the way a canal captain would think of it: the first Saturday in December, 1961. The moment you see it, you cannot unsee it. It is the lock they shut twenty-eight years ago, on the day they finished. The only problem is that you see this at ten past nine on Friday morning. That is one hour and ten minutes after the barge has left.

Nobody with the authority to stop it is standing by the winding pool on Friday morning. Your folder of evidence is in a bag on the kitchen table at home. The store room is cleared by twenty past eight, and the skip goes past the cafe at nine. The padlock, which you thought was the whole problem, was never the real problem at all.

Eleven bits of gear, a room in the community centre, one evening a week, and one adult willing to take formal charge of it all. Every one of those things already exists in this basin, except the last one. Finding that person is the one job you cannot do. It has to be asked for, out loud, in public.

choices.label: Hold the Lock Run on the first Saturday.
Walk the Run with whoever turns up.
Get all six plates back where they belong.

nodes.body: A photo with twenty-one names pencilled on the back is one damp winter away from being twenty-one total strangers. A printed board fixed inside the lock-keeper's hut costs less than the clearance barge would have. It would mean those people stand together, in the dry, for as long as the hut stands.

choices.label: Put the compass back in its case and keep it.
Get every last thing to where it belongs.
Let the store room be emptied once it is listed.
