nodes.body: There is a name stencilled inside the lid of one wooden case, and it is not on the 1961 photograph. That means it belonged to either a later crew member, or a much earlier one. Either way, somebody in the basin today still shares that surname. You just have to find them before the weekend.

choices.label: Stand and watch the skip go.
Wait until somebody in charge notices.
Try the lock one more time and go home.

nodes.body: A signature, a typed list of items, a proper date, and two copies for the file. It takes twenty dull minutes that nobody really wants to spend at the end of a week like this. But it also settles the question of who owns what, legally and for good, for the next thirty years. This is the paperwork that stops the next clearance.

choices.label: Hold the Lock Run on the first Saturday.
Walk the Run with whoever turns up.
Get all six plates back where they belong.

nodes.body: A minute book from 1934, a run of old programmes, and two boxes of photos make a proper archive, not just a sad pile in a damp room. An archive gets a shelf, a catalogue number, and someone with a job title who is officially meant to keep it safe. Aisha writes the number on a sticker and smiles.

choices.label: Put the compass back in its case and keep it.
Get every last thing to where it belongs.
Let the store room be emptied once it is listed.

nodes.body: Six plates, a photocopied map drawn in your neatest handwriting, and a short piece in the local paper. By the next Saturday, people are walking the whole route with a piece of paper. They have lived by this basin for forty years and never knew where the old Lock Run went. They keep stopping to read the plates out loud.

choices.label: Stand and watch the skip go.
Wait until somebody in charge notices.
Try the lock one more time and go home.

nodes.body: It came from a big sale at the boatyard at the end of the season. It cost one pound and fifty pence. It is the only thing in this whole, big hunt that is truly just yours. That means it is the one choice in the whole story that nobody else gets to make.

choices.label: Hold the Lock Run on the first Saturday.
Walk the Run with whoever turns up.
Get all six plates back where they belong.

nodes.body: You walk to eleven front doors, one history centre desk, one lock-side cafe, one waterways depot, and one very busy common room. Saying your last thank-yous in person takes a whole afternoon. But it is the part everyone will recall later. They will recall it more clearly than the padlock, and more fondly than the barge.

choices.label: Put the compass back in its case and keep it.
Get every last thing to where it belongs.
Let the store room be emptied once it is listed.

nodes.body: A date on a poster is a quiet but solid promise. Just six people with three bits of old gear and a copied map can keep it. The Lock Run always takes place on the first Saturday in December. That day is exactly eleven weeks away. You count them out on the calendar and circle the day in red.

choices.label: Stand and watch the skip go.
Wait until somebody in charge notices.
Try the lock one more time and go home.

nodes.body: Nineteen people come to the first practice in the community hall. Eleven of them have never even held a fog horn before. The sound they make is truly and gladly awful. Bill Hurst sits at the front on a plastic chair. His stick rests between his knees. He says, loud enough for all to hear, that this is just how the last one started, too.

ending.title: The Canal Lock Run, Second Time

nodes.body: A proper board with carved letters goes up inside the lock-keeper's hut roof. It has twenty-one names from 1961 on it, and another eleven names from 1998. Four last names appear on both lists. People walking their dogs stop to read it in the light rain. That pause, that tiny moment of wanting to know, is the whole, simple point of writing things on boards.

The name inside the wooden case belongs to a grandmother who lives nearby. She used to carry lamps on the run until she was nineteen. For fifty years she has never once said a word about it out loud. She takes the case back into her hallway and holds it for a moment. Then, after a quiet two weeks of thinking, she brings it along to a Thursday practice.

ending.title: A Case With a Name In It

nodes.body: Two copies, one signed by the trust and one by the community centre. A typed list of eleven items and a date. It is all done on a quiet Tuesday evening in the centre hall. People from the moorings watch from chairs at the back. These are the least tense twenty minutes of the whole two weeks. And this is the only reason the whole plan does not fall apart later.

A minute book from 1934. Four hundred curling photos, a run of printed programmes, and one small card with THE LOCK RUN on it. All are logged, given a number, and put on a shelf. Every sheet has a date stamp on the back. Aisha puts a photo of the compass in the glass case by the door. Under it she places a small, neat sign.

Deniz leaves the brass plate bare. He just moves the heavy menu board one foot to the left. Now it sits right above the sugar station. For about a month, people come to the cafe just to look at a bit of canal brass. While they are there, they end up buying chips. Then the visits slowly stop. The plate simply becomes part of the wall again.

ending.title: The Plate Under the Menu Board

nodes.body: The story runs on Friday. It sits under a photo of an empty, swept store room and a skip on the barge. It is a good piece about something sad that had already taken place. Four people write in to the paper. They say they would gladly have helped, if only someone had known to ask them on Tuesday.

Eleven people, one borrowed fog horn, a copied map, and six brass plates. The little group stops at all six locks in the bitter cold. They sound the horn at each one. It is played badly but with a lot of heart. More people follow it around the basin than anyone had thought. Half of them are under twelve. The echo off the water is the best sound you have ever heard.

Forty people walk the whole route one October Saturday. They follow a man of eighty-four. He stops at every plate, leans on his stick, and says just what used to be there. At the lock-keeper's hut there is no plate at all. Everyone just stands in the tea room car park and listens. By then, the story is more important than the brass.

Five plates go back onto five waiting walls. They use the right, matching screws. The sixth plate was missing. A retired engineer on the industrial estate cuts a brand new one in brass. He will not take any money for it. The new plate goes onto the tea room wall. It fits right in the clean, perfect rectangle of brick that has been waiting there, empty, for twenty-eight years.

ending.title: Six Plates Back on Six Walls

nodes.body: The compass goes back into its case. The card is folded into eighths beside it. The case lives on your shelf. You take it out about once a week. You trace the scratched arrows with your thumb and put it back. It is the only object in the whole story that ends up exactly where it started. But now it means something fully different.

ending.title: The Compass Goes Back in Its Case

nodes.body: Horns and lamps go to the community hall. Paper goes to the history centre. The photo goes to the moorings. Plates go to the walls. The card goes to the archive with a small typed note saying who found it. This takes three quiet weeks of small, dull tasks. By the end, nothing is left stuffed in a bag under a bed. Everything is in a place where it can be found again.

The store room is brought out onto the grass. It gets listed and photographed. Then it is sorted into 'keep' and 'skip' piles. Two removal men are paid by the hour. Against all odds, they find the history very interesting. The brick room under the hut ends the week swept, dry, and empty. It is ready for whatever happens next.

ending.title: The Store Room, Empty and Listed

nodes.body: The skip leaves the basin at nine on Friday morning. It holds a heavy fog horn and four wooden cases. They are buried under old paint tins and rotten rope. A photo of it going is taken from the lock gate. But the local paper will not print it. There is nothing else to say. The whole story ends there, in the back of a barge.

Three different adults could have stopped the clearance if they had known. They had the power to pause it. But no one told them. Asking for help on Wednesday felt like a big, scary thing. It turns out to be much simpler. On Monday, all three of them say so, one after the other. Their quiet talks are ones you will remember for a long time.

The last order is wrong. The wheels go back to zero with a run of small, hopeless clicks. The trail ran from a cardboard box in a rain-soaked boatyard. It went through six walls and sixty years of forgetting. It ends here, at a cold steel door in a silent basin. A barge is booked for the morning. You put the compass in your pocket and walk home in the dark.

ending.title: The Trail Ends at a Steel Door
